blocks.p: I got a question from a listener named Katie that I want to address. It's about shame and anger, and how to deal with them in a polyvagal-informed way. She wrote:
"Hi Justin. I have learned a lot from your videos and am grateful for them. I'm not in a group or workshop, so I hope you'll feel free to ignore this question out of the blue from a stranger."
I got you, Katie. This is a great question, and I was actually looking forward to addressing this one.
Katie asks: "My question is, is it possible to pendulate between dorsal vagal and sympathetic states?"
Let's pause here to make sure we know what we're talking about. We'll talk about this in very cartoony, one-dimensional terms.

Dorsal vagal corresponds with shutdown. That is a limp collapse. We shut down when we cannot be safe, run away, or fight a danger. When our body perceives that we're in a life-threatening scenario, it will collapse. It will play dead. That's what we'll call a dorsal vagal response. Day to day, it looks like depression.
Sympathetic states would be flight and fight. That's where we're trying to run away, or be aggressive, in order to deal with a danger.

She goes on: "I ask because one of my teachers (who's not working in a Polyvagal Theory framework) suggested that anger is the most powerful antidote to shame, and they suggested an exercise in which one would move back and forth between the feeling of shame and the feeling of anger so the two feelings could 'touch.'"
I'm going to cut this off there, because that is concerning to me.

How do I say this delicately? When therapists don't have a framework they're working from, a lot of times they make it up as they go along. I don't mean to insinuate that your teacher is doing that. I don't know your teacher. But we kind of think, "Well, this could be helpful," so we run with it. There's plenty of room to innovate within the mental health world, but we don't want to make things up completely.

The problem is that therapists are more likely, though definitely not every time, to come at the issues our clients bring us from a well-regulated place. I hope we're more likely to be in a place where we have lots of empathy and compassion, healthy boundaries, critical thinking, and a solutions focus. With that, we can help our clients solve problems, and also feel deeply into their emotions. Hopefully we have a wide range of skills we can use with our clients, and also the internal capacity to be with our clients no matter what they bring up, and to use those skills.

So in general, I hope therapists are coming at these issues with a more well-regulated nervous system than their clients have. That's kind of what clients come to us for: someone more regulated, who has the skills to help them.

So therapists, and not just therapists, but coaches or anybody in the wellness sphere, often look at problems from a well-regulated state. And they'll say things like, "Well, just stop doing that," or "Just do this," or "Switch up your structure." But those little ideas are not always great fits for clients. They're often overwhelming. From a well-regulated place, it's like, "Well, duh, just do this differently." I'm not saying all therapists do this, of course, but I'm sure some do.

So with shame and collapse, someone in a well-regulated place can say, "Let me feel into my shame and feel into my collapse," and be able to handle both of those things, and maybe make them, quote unquote, touch. I'm not sure what that means, but touch.

The problem is that we're working with clients who are not in a well-regulated place. That's why they're coming in for help. If a client comes in and we ask them to feel into their shutdown, that is a lot. That is not easy. None of us were taught this stuff as kids. And I think there's a degree of co-regulation that we're probably all missing out on, and therefore a degree of self-regulation, because of all kinds of top-down structures, family, culture, traumas, and incidents that challenge our ability to self-regulate.

For someone who comes into therapy lacking the skills, lacking self-regulation, lacking a history of co-regulation, lacking the ability to look inward and even be curious about what they're feeling, asking them to feel into their shutdown state is not realistic. It is potentially retraumatizing. Asking them to feel into, talk about, or think about their shame is not realistic. That is potentially retraumatizing. So asking them to do a really difficult skill like pendulation, between these two very difficult experiences, is not realistic, and I would argue potentially retraumatizing.

Actual pendulation is when we shift between a state of safety and a state of defense. Peter Levine calls it pendulation, and I think he calls the safety piece of it resourcing. I just refer to it as a safety experience that we can feel into, hang on to, and anchor into. And there's a defensive experience that we can choose to feel into when we're ready to, when we're curious enough to do so.

So pendulation, as I teach it and practice it, is something we do from a very anchored state of safety, only when we are ready and willing and curious and open. Then we go into the defensive activation. That could be stuck defensive activation, but that might be the most difficult.

The way I teach it, we feel into whatever the most present moment defensive activation is. So if someone feels a little anxious about practicing the skill of pendulation, well, voila, that's the feeling we're going to feel into: anxious, or antsy, or nervous. Rather than pushing through that into shame or into shutdown, we probably have to practice with just feeling antsy about the whole thing in the first place. If you can handle that, then we can move forward slowly.

So asking someone to feel into shame and shutdown, and to pendulate between the two of those without first having the anchoring in safety, is not realistic. For someone who's well-regulated and can tolerate that level of activation, sure, maybe. But for a therapy client, for someone in a dysregulated, traumatized state, I personally don't think it's a good idea whatsoever.
Katie goes on: "We were supposed to start with anger and then call up shame."
I'm going to pause here. There's a difference between anger and empowerment. Some people might call empowerment healthy anger, which is fine. I call it empowerment.

When we're just angry, we're not going to be curious about our anger. We're not going to be curious about our shame. We're not going to have the self-compassion to pendulate between these two things. We're not even going to be curious about how much safety we have, or are lacking, in that moment. So if we're just angry, then no, that's not especially helpful.

But if we have an anchoring in safety first, and then welcome some anger, maybe that's what "touch" means. If we pendulate between safety and anger, those two things can combine or merge. It's a self-regulation process. Once you're anchored in safety enough, curious enough, and present enough, they'll kind of do their own thing, and you'll see them merge together in a sense.

Once we have an anchoring in safety, allow anger or fight activation, and pendulate between the two, that will turn into empowerment. So it's kind of like anger, but it's really not. It's activated, maybe with a bit of fight activation, but very anchored in safety. From this state, we can have healthy boundaries. We can say no and stick to it. We can have clear and positive expectations for ourselves and others. All that kind of healthy boundaries stuff, and speaking up for yourself.

From empowerment, sure, we might be able to go into shame. We might be able to allow some of that. But the necessary piece is the safety state, which then combines with anger, which then turns into empowerment, which then maybe opens up the potential for looking at shame, if that person wants to.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.p: Katie continues: "We were supposed to start with anger, then call upon shame, back to anger, then back and forth, and so forth."
That's a lot to ask from someone who is not well-regulated, and who maybe cannot even accept co-regulation. For therapy students in class, maybe you can handle that, but it's a lot.

She says: "I've been trying unsuccessfully to do this exercise, and I'm wondering how to explain what might not be working for me in terms of the autonomic nervous system. I can call upon anger, but moving from that into shame feels like such a downregulation that I can't hang on to any of the anger while in a shame state."
Yeah, Katie, that's a lot to ask. I think anyone would have a hard time with this, and it's not because they're broken or defective. It's just a lot. It's a tall order.

As far as the autonomic nervous system goes, there are a couple of possibilities. If someone is able to welcome sympathetic flight and fight more easily, then either they have a strong anchoring in safety and can now allow some of that, which is great and shows a lot of self-regulation, or they have lingering flight and fight activation that they can easily call upon. They might live more in safety, or in flight and fight activation, and then calling upon shutdown might be a challenge.

Or this could be someone who easily goes into shutdown, but has enough safety that the shutdown is contained. When they try to feel into flight and fight, they can do it, but they can't maintain it, because the safety state isn't active or strong enough. So trying to go back down into shutdown is really just more of a dorsal collapse at that point. They can't hang on to safety, and they can't hang on to flight and fight.

I'm doing the best I can to frame this in autonomic nervous system terms, but this is really not a technique I would use personally. So it's hard to say in general what could be happening within someone, but those are a couple of possibilities, I think.

Katie asks: "You talk about pendulating between autonomic states sometimes, but I think usually it's between safety and something else. If you're willing to help me reframe the trouble I'm having with this exercise in Polyvagal terms, I'd be grateful. Or is there a more Polyvagal-informed version of working specifically with anger and shame that you might suggest?"

When it comes to the polyvagal-informed aspect of it, it's the safety state. We have to have the safety state active enough, and then tiptoe into the flight and fight activation, or into the shame, which probably has a lot of dorsal activation to it. That's really the polyvagal-informed aspect of this: how much safety do you have active, and is your safety state capable of balancing or sustaining the flight and fight activation if you choose to feel into it?

The pendulation aspect is not a polyvagal prescriptive thing. That's more of a Somatic Experiencing, Peter Levine kind of thing. I'm sure other people do it as well, and I do a lot of pendulation work myself. It's a somatic exercise, not exactly a polyvagal one. But I think we have to have the safety aspect of it.

The way I teach this stuff, that's the priority. I know people want to feel into and relieve their stuck defensive state, but the priority is starting in safety, ending in safety, and maintaining safety while pendulating. That is the absolute priority. If you're not doing that, you're significantly running a risk of dysregulation.

I'm not trying to fearmonger, but it's a real concern. If you are not prioritizing safety, you are running a risk of dysregulation, and a risk of retraumatization. Once your safety state comes off, your body is potentially back in a very scary moment from the past, or experiencing a whole new level of dysregulation in the present moment. That's not helpful, and it's probably going to dissuade someone from trying this skill again.

The last thing I'll put forth is that I consider pendulation an advanced skill. The pathway I teach goes from A to Z, from learning the Polyvagal Theory all the way to pendulation, and a little beyond that, into how to act on impulses that come up from pendulation. On my scale of knowledge and skills, pendulation is way toward the end. It's a very advanced skill, especially if you're doing it by yourself.

When I'm leading people through it live, we do a limited number of pendulations. We'll do safety, defense, safety, defense, safety. We'll call that four pendulations, and that's the maximum. And that's with me leading someone through it. By yourself, it's even more difficult.

So before someone pendulates, I want to see that they can do other things first. I want to see that they know how to balance defensive activation. Before balancing, I like to see that they can do something I call imagery and invitation. Before that, can you normalize? Before that, can you validate what you're going through? Before that, can you anchor into safety?

So to pull it back to where I began: from a well-regulated place, we'd say, "Just stop doing the thing you're doing," or "Just use this pendulation skill," or "Just feel into your anger and your shame." But that's from a well-regulated place. Katie, you're a therapy student, and your clients are going to come to you from a place that is not well-regulated.

Pendulation is a great skill, but it's not the first answer, not the first step for people. If you're well-regulated enough, sure. But a lot of times we're starting from zero, or we're undoing a lot of stuff we learned in the past that was not helpful, and we have to start from zero in a sense.
